summary: Reports on the ARPANET Users Interest Working Group, a new group that grew out of a Boston meeting in May 1973 after BBN's Resource Sharing Workshop. The meeting served as a forum for users to air complaints, swap information and make proposals.

eli5.summary: After a big workshop, network users met to share what bugged them and what they wanted. This is the report of that meeting.

questions: arpanet users interest working group meeting 1973
subtitle: A May 1973 meeting where network users aired their wishes for the system

tldr.problem: ARPANET users faced many frustrations: difficult documentation, too many different command languages, poor information sharing, and no systematic way to report problems.
tldr.mechanism: Fifteen network people met in Boston after a resource-sharing workshop to identify and discuss user concerns, voice proposals for improvement, and coordinate efforts to make ARPANET more usable.
tldr.outcome: The group identified thirteen major areas of user concern and created work teams to draft specifications for a Common Command Language, a simple editor, and a handbook for new users.

today: RFC 585 is a historical record of the first USING meeting and the extensive feedback about what users needed from ARPANET. Many of the issues identified—documentation quality, command standardisation, error handling, and accessibility for new users—remained important concerns in network design for years.

sections.title: A Meeting to Hear User Voices
sections.content:
The ARPANET Users Interest Working Group (USING) grew out of a meeting held in Boston on May 22 and 23, 1973, following BBN's Resource Sharing Workshop. Fifteen attendees from across the network—including people from UCLA, BBN, UCSD, NIC, NASA, MIT, MIT-Multics and Harvard—came together under co-chairs Dave Crocker (UCLA-NMC) and Nancy Neigus (BBN).

The meeting was understood as a forum for network users to air complaints, exchange information, voice desires, and present concrete proposals for user-oriented network capabilities. The group committed to lobbying on behalf of user interests, promoting resource sharing, improving user interfaces and studying standardisation.
sections.eli5: Fifteen network people met to swap complaints and ideas about what would make the network better to use.

sections.title: Thirteen Major Categories of User Concern
sections.content:
The group systematically created a list of topics directly relevant to users, then discussed them in detail. The thirteen categories spanned documentation quality and information sharing (including a proposal for a Network Yellow Pages), standardisation (especially a common command language so users did not have to learn twenty different command languages), site performance measurement and software certification, user feedback mechanisms, better error messages, resource tailoring for different user skill levels, personal information management, accounting procedures, trial usage and browsing, prelogon facilities, remote user facilitation, transportability of resources between sites, and network utilities.

Each category included multiple recommendations. For example, documentation should avoid jargon, include version and author information, and be available in both online (searchable) and offline (indexed) forms. Some recommendations were ambitious and would take years to implement, but the group noted them anyway.
sections.eli5: They went through everything that bothered users: guides that were hard to read, commands that were different at every site, no way to say what was broken, and needing special help to move files around.

sections.title: Next Steps and Concrete Work
sections.content:
The group assigned concrete work to subgroups. Neigus, Crocker and Iseli were tasked with drafting a detailed scope, objectives, goals and priorities for USING itself, to be submitted for member approval. MITRE was asked to design a New User's Packet. Bowles, Hathaway and Stoughton volunteered to outline preliminary specifications for a Network Common Command Language Protocol that would work with both interactive and batch systems. Padlipsky agreed to produce specifications for a simple, standard editor (which came to be called NETED) that server hosts could implement.

A general Users Group (NIC ident = USERS) was to be formed to allow anyone to monitor user-oriented activities and receive reports through the ARPANET News. The group planned to meet again in the fall of 1973 at the Network Information Center in Menlo Park, California.
sections.eli5: They split up the work: some would write down the official charter, some would make a guide for new users, some would design a universal command system, and some would design a simple editor everyone could use.
